medical.family: Acute, emergency, pulmonary and critical care
medical.trackType: Clinical physician fellowship (institutional fellowship in a clinical field; not a distinct board specialty in reviewed ABEM certification sources)
boardNames: American Board of Emergency Medicine (ABEM) — Emergency Medicine (underlying specialty; not a Global Emergency Medicine certification)
medical.boardStatus: ABEM’s current public subspecialty-certification list does not list Global Emergency Medicine. The BWH fellowship is an institutional clinical fellowship, not a separate board-designated specialty. General ABEM Emergency Medicine qualifying/certifying examinations apply only to candidates who independently meet ABEM requirements; no separate Global Emergency Medicine board examination was identified in the reviewed official sources. The ABEM 2022 EM Model remains the published general EM examination content basis on the date checked; it is not a Global EM blueprint.
medical.boardEligibilityNotice: The current BWH programme page says applicants must be board certified or board eligible in Emergency Medicine when they begin the fellowship. ABEM separately requires qualifying accredited/approved EM residency completion and its medical-licensure policy for its board-eligible status. This educational course does not confer ABEM eligibility, certification, institutional eligibility, licensure, or examination readiness.

officialProgrammes.name: BWH Global Emergency Medicine Fellowship
officialProgrammes.publicCurriculumNotes: The current MGB-hosted programme page describes a clinical physician fellowship designed for emergency physicians. It states two years (one year for fellows with an MPH), approximately 3–4 months/year in international field projects, Harvard T.H. Chan public-health training, research, clinical attending practice at BWH and BWH Faulkner, and a board-certified/board-eligible in Emergency Medicine entry expectation. The public page is a descriptive page, not a full syllabus or ACGME accreditation record.

medical.programmeSourceScope: Exact institutional variant preserved from the MED-X100 packet: Brigham and Women’s Hospital — “BWH Global Emergency Medicine Fellowship.” The current MGB-hosted page titles it “Fellowship in Global Emergency Medicine” and also calls it the “Harvard Global Emergency Medicine Fellowship.” The linked older programme-description PDF supplies additional detail (six curriculum areas, clinical FTE/shifts, MPH competencies, field placements and research), but may not reflect every current practice. Neither source is a public institutional lecture list or board blueprint. The public record makes this a physician clinical fellowship with research and public-health components—not a combined EM/MPH residency, stand-alone research-only position, generic directory category, or non-physician supplement. The verified public sources do not establish ACGME accreditation of this particular fellowship; none is claimed.
sourceCaveats: Reviewed the current MGB-hosted programme page and its linked programme-description PDF; older PDF can differ from current public page. No unpublished curriculum has been inferred.
Official program description and board examination materials serve different purposes. ABEM’s exam structure is general Emergency Medicine, not a Global EM specialty exam.
Global EM fellowship selection and board eligibility vary by program/jurisdiction; the quoted BWH expectation is programme-specific and dated to the public page accessed.

Clinical treatment details are deliberately limited to structured high-level case reasoning. WHO BEC is first-contact training and not a substitute for specialist judgment or locally approved protocols. WHO’s BEC page notes updates to postpartum-haemorrhage recommendations in November 2025; consult current guidance before teaching such specifics.
Human clinical review is not performed. Clinical resources require date-specific review by qualified local clinicians before educational deployment.

No external lecture runtime reached the verification threshold. Public YouTube links surfaced through search are not sufficient duration evidence; YouTube metadata probes were blocked/intermittent. Therefore verified hours are zero and the genuine video gap is 36 hours. Planned scripts/clips are production plans only, not rendered, uploaded, or ready videos.

Case links are for viewing only; patient-level cases/images are not copied. A free-to-view case does not automatically permit rehosting, and site-specific case attribution and privacy conditions still apply.

This independent educational curriculum grants no Harvard/Brigham affiliation, accredited training, degree, licensure, board eligibility, board certification, procedure competence, deployment authorization, or guaranteed exam passing.

topicGaps: A full 36 hours of verified, free, public lecture recordings specific to global EM were not confirmed.
No verified runtime ledger for the indexed Global EM Grand Rounds video or otherwise useful BEC videos.
No public BWH full lecture archive or source curriculum was found; proprietary, login-only, paid courses and in-person content are not counted.

medical.sourceReviewNote: Source-cited research and automated checks; not clinician validation or exam-passing prediction.

practiceQuestions.stem: A district-level review is intended to map the emergency-care continuum using the WHO Emergency Care System Framework. Which pathway best matches its scope?

options.text: Emergency department only, ending at discharge
Scene/first contact through transport and emergency unit to early inpatient care
Ambulance dispatch only
Only the intensive care unit

practiceQuestions.rationale: WHO describes essential emergency-care functions at the scene, during transport, through the emergency unit and early inpatient care. A single hospital department misses upstream and downstream links.

practiceQuestions.stem: A course designer wants a free WHO resource for first-contact workers on a structured initial approach to acute illness and injury in a limited-resource setting. Which source is the closest fit, with what caveat?

options.text: WHO/ICRC Basic Emergency Care; it is first-contact open training, not a specialist fellowship or substitute for local protocols
The ABEM subspecialty list; it certifies a BEC provider
The Sphere Handbook; it is a board exam question bank
A private residency lecture archive

practiceQuestions.rationale: WHO describes BEC as open-access first-contact training; its availability does not create a Global EM board certification.

practiceQuestions.stem: After a sudden-onset disaster, an overseas emergency medical team offers to deploy before contacting local authorities. Under WHO EMT guidance, what is the best next step?

options.text: Deploy immediately because extra capacity is always beneficial
Wait for the affected country’s request/acceptance and follow registration, licensing, coordination and tasking processes
Set up independently and notify the host country after opening
Assume team self-classification grants national licensure

practiceQuestions.rationale: WHO EMT guidance describes formal acceptance/approval, registration and licensing, and tasking/coordination under the affected country’s response; uncoordinated teams can cause harm.

practiceQuestions.stem: A local partner asks whether a handover-improvement project is working. Which proposed process indicator is most interpretable?

options.text: “Better handovers happened often”
Number of referrals, with no time period or denominator
Transfers with agreed handover elements documented divided by all eligible inter-facility transfers in a defined period, with missing-record limitations reported
Survival increased, attributed solely to the project without comparison

practiceQuestions.rationale: A defined numerator, denominator, period and source make a process measure interpretable. The indicator alone does not establish causal effect on survival.

practiceQuestions.stem: A multinational emergency-medicine team begins a minimal-risk health-services study. Which practice best fits IFEM’s research-ethics framing?

options.text: Let the visiting investigator alone set priorities and retain the data
Agree with local collaborators on the question, permissions, data stewardship, dissemination, and fair contribution/authorship before collection
Collect identifiable patient data first and request approval later
Avoid discussing local benefit if the study is publishable

practiceQuestions.rationale: IFEM emphasizes mutually beneficial relationships; early collaboration, review, data governance and fair dissemination support reciprocal research.

practiceQuestions.stem: A learner evaluates a possible clinical project for displaced people. Which approach is most consistent with respectful, safe educational practice?

options.text: Assume all members of the population share the same preferences
Use an interpreter where needed, protect privacy, ask about barriers and preferences, and plan only realistic locally available follow-up
Ask a child relative to interpret sensitive information as a default
Collect identifying stories for class because the setting is humanitarian

practiceQuestions.rationale: Use respectful, interpreter-centered communication, protect privacy and plan around real barriers without stereotyping or unnecessary disclosure.

practiceQuestions.stem: A team wants to describe the proportion of eligible clinic visits involving an acute-care syndrome across two sites. What is the key first step before comparing percentages?

options.text: Use the number of staff as the denominator at each site
Define the syndrome/case criteria, eligible visit denominator, time window and completeness similarly at both sites
Remove any site with missing data without reporting it
Call the difference causal

practiceQuestions.rationale: A comparable descriptive estimate requires explicit criteria, denominators, aligned periods and transparent missing-data limits; it is not causal evidence.

practiceQuestions.stem: A programme introduces staff training and observes a higher rate of documented referral handovers afterward. What is the most defensible initial interpretation?

options.text: Training proved that patient mortality fell
The measured process changed over time; consider documentation changes, case mix, missingness and other causes before causal claims
The programme has no value because only process indicators were measured
The result grants clinical credentialing

practiceQuestions.rationale: An uncontrolled before-after observation supports description but does not identify causal effects or patient outcomes.

practiceQuestions.stem: An educator proposes embedding multiple Radiopaedia images in a paid restricted-access course because the cases can be viewed without paying. What is appropriate?

options.text: Free-to-view automatically permits commercial redistribution
Link only unless permission is confirmed; respect attribution, share-alike and noncommercial conditions, as paid/restricted courses may need additional permission
Remove creator attribution to make the slide original
Use images without checking case-level privacy or license

practiceQuestions.rationale: Radiopaedia describes noncommercial attribution/share-alike conditions and says paid or restricted courses require additional permission. This course links only and copies no images.

practiceQuestions.stem: A learner finishes this independent Global EM self-study course and asks whether this makes them ABEM board-eligible or qualifies them for a Global EM board exam. What is correct?

options.text: Yes, the course automatically grants both statuses
ABEM lists Global EM as a subspecialty exam
No. ABEM eligibility requires separate qualifying accredited/approved EM training and licensure review; its listed subspecialties do not include Global EM
Yes, if all 36 planned video hours are completed

practiceQuestions.rationale: ABEM eligibility is based on qualifying training and licensure review. Its public subspecialty list does not include Global EM; planned videos confer no credential.

assignment.title: Fictional remote incident plan and evidence brief
assignment.instructions: Create a clearly fictional, text-only scenario. Submit a risk/scene map; focused assessment and differential; stabilization and evacuation options; reassessment trigger; 90-second handover; and a 500-word evidence note with at least three current authoritative sources. Do not include copied patient photos or records; do not prescribe individualized real-patient care or describe unauthorized procedures.

rubric.anchors: 25: organized, uncertainty-aware and appropriately prioritized; 13: major omissions; 0: unsafe certainty.
20: terrain, timing, communication and deterioration triggers integrated; 10: partial; 0: no workable safety plan.
20: authoritative sources accurately mapped and date-checked; 10: mixed quality or weak mapping; 0: unsupported claims.
20: scope/consent/privacy and concise handover respected; 10: partial; 0: unsafe or privacy-violating.
15: meaningful debrief/QI question and explicit limitations; 8: superficial; 0: absent.

assignment.passingInterpretation: Formative course rubric only; not a validated examination predictor or certification.

assessment.formative: Unit concept maps, case reflections, multiple-choice rationales and peer discussion prompts.
assessment.summative: Fictional incident plan (100-point rubric) plus 10 original practice questions; mastery suggests 80% for personal review, not board readiness.
assessment.limits: No patient-care performance examination, observed procedural assessment, board exam, or validated psychometric instrument is provided.

studyHours.basis: Planning estimate for reading, 12 units, assignments, case review and exam reflection; not observed lecture time or a clinical competency measure.

medical.programmeSourceScope: The official packet names the MGH Fellowship in Wilderness Medicine. MGH’s own SPEAR page is a duplicate official presentation of the same programme, preserved as a page variant rather than a second fellowship. MGH describes a 1–2 year clinical physician fellowship for EM residency graduates; public activities include field medicine, ED clinical practice, teaching and research. The public page links an institutional curriculum PDF but not a complete lecture archive. WMS lists the MGH fellowship as not WMS-certified (as checked 2026-10-07). SAEM provides an approval pathway and requires an interactive directory for live programme status; MGH-specific SAEM approval was not publicly confirmed. Wilderness medicine fellowships are non-ACGME-certified per WMS; do not confuse the prerequisite ACGME-accredited EM residency with accreditation of the fellowship itself.
sourceCaveats: The MGH programme page is authoritative for its stated programme identity and published design, but it does not disclose every rotation, assessment, hour or fellowship lecture.
WMS current map lists MGH as not WMS-certified. SAEM approval-specific MGH status could not be confirmed from public static text; no inference made.
ABEM/ABMS directory review did not identify a wilderness-medicine board certificate/exam; absence in these current directories is not a statement about every non-board credential worldwide.
WMS FAWM is a voluntary Academy designation with membership, credits, experience and review; not a board credential or licensure.
This online self-study curriculum is unaffiliated and is not accredited physician training. No human clinical review was performed.

medical.sourceReviewNote: Source-cited research and automated checks; not clinician validation or exam-passing prediction.

practiceQuestions.stem: A lowlander ascends rapidly to a sleeping altitude above 3,400 m and develops headache, nausea and fatigue within hours. No ataxia or respiratory distress is reported. Which is the safest immediate ascent decision?

options.text: Continue ascending if pulse oximetry is normal
Stop further ascent and assess severity; consider descent if worsening or unable to function
Diagnose HACE from headache alone
Treat with an OTC oxygen canister and continue

practiceQuestions.rationale: The WMS/CDC context supports AMS after ascent; do not continue ascending with symptoms. Normal pulse oximetry does not exclude illness. Worsening symptoms, severe illness, or inability to descend safely requires escalation; no diagnosis is established by this fictional vignette alone.

practiceQuestions.stem: A person at altitude develops confusion and a wide-based gait after recent ascent. What feature makes this an emergency altitude syndrome rather than uncomplicated AMS?

options.text: Headache alone
Ataxia and altered mental status suggesting HACE
A normal skin temperature
A pulse oximeter value without context

practiceQuestions.rationale: Ataxia and encephalopathy/altered mentation are red flags for HACE. Suspected HACE warrants urgent descent and treatment/escalation; other dangerous causes such as head injury, hypoglycemia, infection or stroke must remain in the differential.

practiceQuestions.stem: A climber with suspected HAPE has severe exertional dyspnea at rest at a remote camp. Which action best reflects current WMS guidance?

options.text: Encourage vigorous walking to the trailhead
Start oxygen if available and initiate descent with minimal exertion; use evacuation support
Wait for a confirmatory chest radiograph before acting
Give a small consumer oxygen can and stop monitoring

practiceQuestions.rationale: For suspected HAPE, oxygen if available and descent are central; minimize exertion and use supported evacuation. Portable hyperbaric chamber may be considered when descent is infeasible/delayed, but should not delay descent. Consumer canisters are not adequate sustained therapy.

practiceQuestions.stem: A frozen foot may thaw during evacuation, but the route is exposed to conditions where it could refreeze. What is the key field decision principle?

options.text: Thaw immediately under any heat source
Avoid thawing if refreezing cannot be prevented; protect from further injury and seek appropriate care
Rub vigorously to restore circulation
Apply snow to prevent blistering

practiceQuestions.rationale: The WMS frostbite summary stresses avoiding refreezing after thawing. If a sustainable rapid water-bath rewarming cannot be maintained, protect the tissue, prevent further trauma and arrange evacuation; avoid rubbing, ice/snow and uncontrolled heat.

practiceQuestions.stem: A remote trauma patient is stable but has a painful suspected long-bone injury. Which principle is most appropriate for a study plan?

options.text: Perform a reduction regardless of training
Immobilize and reassess distal function, protect from exposure, and choose evacuation with trained clinical oversight
Leave the limb unsupported until imaging is available
Use the highest-risk route to minimize time

practiceQuestions.rationale: Field stabilization, repeated assessment, packaging and evacuation are core topics. Reduction/procedure decisions require credentialed training, local protocols, supervision and patient-specific assessment; this course does not authorize them.

practiceQuestions.stem: During a water rescue, what is the first priority for a responder before entering the water?

options.text: Immediate unprotected entry
Scene and rescuer safety; activate an appropriate rescue system and avoid creating a second victim
Collect a detailed medication history
Wait for a physician to arrive before calling rescue

practiceQuestions.rationale: Wilderness EMS and rescue begin with scene/rescuer safety and systems activation. A rescuer should not enter water without appropriate training/equipment. Drowning care after safe access prioritizes ventilation/resuscitation per current professional protocols.

practiceQuestions.stem: A diver with neurologic symptoms after surfacing is being evaluated at a remote site. Which response is most defensible?

options.text: Assume anxiety and continue the dive trip
Stop diving, support ABCs, activate emergency transport/medical consultation and consider decompression illness in the differential
Require a local imaging study before contacting specialists
Treat as a marine sting without exposure history

practiceQuestions.rationale: Neurologic symptoms after a dive require urgent evaluation for decompression illness and other causes. This course provides conceptual triage only; contact emergency services and dive-medicine/hyperbaric expertise rather than attempting unsupervised treatment.

practiceQuestions.stem: A hiker is bitten by an unidentified snake. Which action is appropriate?

options.text: Cut and suck the wound
Keep the patient safe, limit exertion, record exposure details without delaying evacuation, and consult poison control/emergency services
Apply ice directly and tightly bind the limb
Catch the snake to identify it

practiceQuestions.rationale: Avoid harmful folk interventions and do not risk another bite. Stabilization, prompt expert consultation and region-appropriate evacuation are essential; do not use unverified species-specific treatment.

practiceQuestions.stem: In an avalanche burial, which variables are most important to initial survival assessment?

options.text: Only the victim’s age
Burial duration, airway patency/air pocket, and traumatic injury along with hypothermia context
Only snow depth
The rescuer’s estimate of oxygen saturation

practiceQuestions.rationale: The open avalanche review identifies burial duration, airway patency, air pocket, snow properties and trauma as major determinants; asphyxia and trauma are common mechanisms. Avoid attributing every arrest to hypothermia.

practiceQuestions.stem: A case presentation uses a published, de-identified clinical photograph that is free to view but lacks a clear reuse license. What should the learner do?

options.text: Download and add it to a course slide
Link to the source and discuss the text; do not copy/rehost the image without permission
Remove the source attribution
Assume open access means unrestricted use

practiceQuestions.rationale: Free-to-view is not a license to reuse. Link to source material; reproduce imagery only when an explicit license or permission allows it, retaining required attribution. Never copy private records or identifiable patient images.

deliverables: A 4-page fictional tabletop incident action brief: situation, assumptions, command/coordination map, operational priorities, resource requests and public-health interfaces.

assessment.format: 12 unit formative case worksheets; 12 original practice questions; final fictional tabletop brief.

medical.boardEligibilityNotice: The MGH programme page says EM residency applicants must have completed an ACGME-accredited EM residency in good standing; other ACGME-accredited specialty graduates may be considered with clinical funding arrangements, and non-ACGME applicants may be eligible with external funding. This is institutional programme eligibility language, not board eligibility. ABMS board eligibility rules for the new subspecialty were not yet published in the cited board notices. Verify directly with boards and programme.

officialProgrammes.name: MGH Disaster Medicine and Healthcare Emergency Management Fellowship
officialProgrammes.publicCurriculumNotes: Official programme page: one-year physician fellowship; states Society for Academic Emergency Medicine approval; four objectives include emergency-management programme development, resource-limited clinical care, leadership, and research. Core topics stated include triage, MCI, HazMat, high-consequence infectious diseases, mass care. Clinical role in MGH or BWH ED is conditional on EM residency pathway and institutional criteria. Public page does not give lecture catalogue or verified didactic hours.

medical.programmeSourceScope: The exact MGH DM-HEM named physician fellowship in the packet was verified on the official programme page. It is neither a generic directory label nor a research-only/non-physician supplement. The institutional programme page calls it a one-year fellowship and asserts SAEM approval; no independent accreditation status beyond that statement is inferred. ACGME EM overview lists seven subspecialties and does not list Disaster Medicine as of 2026-10-07. ABMS approval of a future/new Disaster Medicine board subspecialty is a separate status from this institution-specific fellowship and from ACGME accreditation. No additional institutional variant found in the supplied packet; do not infer a Johns Hopkins or separate Harvard-wide programme.
sourceCaveats: MGH claims SAEM approval; no separate accreditor source was retrieved, and this is not ACGME accreditation.
ABMS subspecialty approval does not itself establish examination launch, individual board eligibility, programme accreditation, or MGH fellowship graduate eligibility.
ACGME Emergency Medicine overview does not list Disaster Medicine among EM subspecialties at date checked; this page alone is not a comprehensive ACGME program-search result.
Disaster Medicine exam content outline was not found in the official ABEM/ABPM notices fetched; do not treat unit domains as official exam blueprint.
NCDMPH says the Disaster Health Core Curriculum is being modernized; cite as a foundation rather than immutable current standard.
Clinical content has not undergone human clinical review; verify current local/jurisdictional protocols.

practiceQuestions.stem: A hospital detects a sudden influx of casualties. Which first planning lens best supports a scalable response?

options.text: Activate predefined all-hazards incident management, establish situational assessment, and align actions with local plans.
Wait until casualty count exceeds a fixed national threshold.
Send every patient to the nearest tertiary ED.
Suspend public health and EMS communications until the incident commander arrives.

practiceQuestions.rationale: All-hazards plans and incident management are designed for scalable, coordinated actions; fixed universal thresholds are not presumed.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which statement most accurately describes ICS?

options.text: It is a standardized command and coordination structure that can scale and interface across agencies.
It replaces clinical professional judgment.
It is only used by fire services.
It assigns the hospital CEO permanent incident command.

practiceQuestions.rationale: FEMA describes ICS principles, structure, roles, and NIMS relationship; operational role assignments are incident-specific.

practiceQuestions.stem: A planning team is reviewing a hospital EOP. Which distinction is sound?

options.text: EMP describes the management program; EOP describes actions and operational response.
EOP is only a list of hazards; EMP is only a patient census.
Both are interchangeable labels with no functional difference.
EOP is a board examination blueprint.

practiceQuestions.rationale: ASPR TRACIE describes the EMP as the administrative framework and EOP as what the facility does during an incident.

practiceQuestions.stem: A radiation incident has been declared and a potentially contaminated patient arrives. Which principle is safest?

options.text: Follow facility incident command, responder safety, contamination control/decontamination protocols, and agent-specific clinical guidance.
Delay all emergency care until the whole incident is characterized.
Assume every person exposed to radiation is externally contaminated.
Use a single antidote before assessing exposure.

practiceQuestions.rationale: CDC training focuses on planning, decontamination, triage, treatment and hypothetical scenarios; avoid unsupported universal treatment.

practiceQuestions.stem: During a mass-casualty event, how should triage be framed educationally?

options.text: A context-dependent, repeatedly reassessed allocation process guided by local protocol and current resources.
A universally invariant algorithm unaffected by resource conditions.
A diagnosis that permanently determines care.
A substitute for command and patient tracking.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Triage is an operational process under changing capacity; the module emphasizes rationale, reassessment and local protocol.

practiceQuestions.stem: A resource allocation decision is ethically defensible when it is:

options.text: Transparent, consistently applied, accountable, proportionate, and documented with relevant clinical/operational facts.
Based on social status or perceived social worth.
Made privately without review.
Presented as a clinical certainty despite missing facts.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Ethical frameworks emphasize fair process, transparency, consistency, accountability and documentation; local legal rules vary.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which is the best use of a healthcare coalition?

options.text: Coordinate information, mutual aid, and resource requests across healthcare partners and public agencies.
Replace local incident command at every facility.
Guarantee unlimited beds and supplies.
Practice only after disasters.

practiceQuestions.rationale: ASPR coalition capabilities emphasize coordination, continuity and medical surge rather than replacing member facility command.

practiceQuestions.stem: In a high-consequence infectious disease concern, a first operational approach should include:

options.text: Prompt recognition, isolation/infection prevention, notification through established channels, and workforce protection.
Wait for definitive laboratory confirmation before using standard precautions.
Send potentially infectious patients through public waiting areas.
Treat every alert as confirmed diagnosis.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Core preparedness actions are designed around risk recognition and safe process while uncertainty is resolved; site-specific protocols control.

practiceQuestions.stem: A hazard vulnerability assessment is primarily used to:

options.text: Prioritize plausible threats and capability gaps to inform mitigation and preparedness planning.
Predict exactly when an event will occur.
Determine board eligibility.
Assign a diagnosis to an individual patient.

practiceQuestions.rationale: HVA informs planning; it is not a precise event forecast.

practiceQuestions.stem: A learner finds a public case PDF online. What is appropriate?

options.text: Link to the source and check item-specific permissions before reproducing; do not copy patient records or images.
Rehost the PDF because viewing it is free.
Assume de-identification permits any reuse.
Remove the source credit and add it to slides.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Free viewing is not a general rehosting license; clinical images and patient records require rights and privacy review.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which evidence supports describing MGH DM-HEM as an institutional clinical physician fellowship?

options.text: MGH page calls it a one-year physician fellowship and describes applicant and clinical experience pathways.
The ABMS subspecialty recognition alone proves ACGME accreditation.
FEMA course catalog lists MGH as an accredited fellowship.
A generic directory category establishes board eligibility.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Official MGB programme page documents identity; ABMS certification approval, ACGME accreditation, and board eligibility are separate determinations.

practiceQuestions.stem: As of the current ABEM/ABPM announcement, which board statement is most accurate?

options.text: ABMS approved Disaster Medicine subspecialty certification with ABEM, ABPM and ABS collaboration; implementation/eligibility specifics were still forthcoming in the cited notices.
MGH fellowship graduates are automatically board-certified.
A separate exam is already open to all physicians.
Disaster Medicine is an ACGME EM subspecialty on the cited current list.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The 2026 announcements establish approval and sponsoring boards but say more details are forthcoming; ACGME page lists different EM subspecialties.

coveredTopics: Formulate a locally supported problem statement.

unitMap.text: Workforce strategy, safety, wellbeing and labor relations
coveredTopics: Assess staffing against demand, workload and safety.
Plan a fair response to conflict and workplace violence.
Choose workforce measures with privacy protections.

unitMap.text: Governance, strategy and interdepartmental relationships
coveredTopics: Map ED and hospital decision rights.
Identify conflicts of interest and resource tradeoffs.

unitMap.text: Policy, regulation, compliance and ethical leadership
coveredTopics: Distinguish statutes, regulations, guidance and local policy.
Recognize when counsel, compliance, privacy, ethics or IRB review is needed.

unitMap.text: Health IT, clinical informatics and responsible innovation
coveredTopics: Create governance checklist for an ED information system change.
Assess alert burden, interoperability, downtime and privacy.
Describe limits and monitoring of analytic/AI tools.

unitMap.text: Health equity, population health, research and scholarly leadership
coveredTopics: Assess outcomes by relevant strata without overinterpreting small cells.
Develop a scholarly question with appropriate oversight.
Synthesize an ethical project and evaluation plan.

medical.family: Acute, emergency, pulmonary and critical care
boardNames: ABEM Emergency Medicine primary certification
ABEM Health Care Administration, Leadership, and Management (HALM) subspecialty examination
ABA, ABFM and ABPM HALM pathways for their respective eligible diplomates
medical.boardStatus: This is a clinical physician fellowship, not a primary specialty board. ABEM administers a separate HALM subspecialty examination; some eligible physicians apply through ABA, ABFM or ABPM. Emergency Medicine primary certification is distinct. MGB public pages do not establish this fellowship is ACGME accredited or meets a HALM pathway.
medical.boardEligibilityNotice: MGB states candidates must be ABEM board-certified or board-eligible before the July 1 start. HALM has separate ABMS certification, active continuing certification, licensure and pathway requirements. ABEM criteria describe ACGME-accredited training and time-limited training-plus-practice routes. No evidence reviewed confirms this specific MGB fellowship qualifies; verify directly. No eligibility is promised.

title: Dermatology Laser and Cosmetic Fellowship
prerequisites: Audience level: dermatology residents/fellows or practicing physicians with prior medical education; not a substitute for MD/DO education.
Recommended prior knowledge: skin anatomy, dermatologic diagnosis, basic photobiology, informed consent and reading of clinical evidence.
Do not attempt device use from this curriculum. Supervised accredited clinical training and institutional laser authorization are outside course scope.
objectives: Explain core laser–tissue interactions and distinguish laser from IPL and other energy-based devices.
Identify diagnostic, patient, device, room and follow-up considerations before a cosmetic procedure.
Critically appraise device evidence and disclose uncertainty, conflict and alternatives.
Describe hazards and safety controls at a conceptual level without claiming operator competence.
Apply inclusive risk reasoning to pigmentary disease, skin of colour and varied treatment goals.

units.title: Laser–tissue interaction and device literacy
objectives: Explain wavelength, chromophore absorption, pulse duration, fluence, spot size, cooling and selective photothermolysis qualitatively.
Compare laser, intense pulsed light, radiofrequency and ultrasound at the level needed to interpret device claims.
topics: Photobiology; laser/device physics; energy-based device distinctions
boardDomains: Photobiology; laser/device physics; energy-based device distinctions
units.boardMappingNote: Educational alignment to broad general dermatology knowledge/procedural-safety domains only; no laser/cosmetic board blueprint or board examination is asserted.
units.casePractice: Map a device specification to a target chromophore and identify which missing device details prevent safe conclusions.
units.assessment: Short-answer concept map: 20 points for correct wavelength/chromophore, pulse/thermal reasoning, optical depth caveat and explicit uncertainty.

units.title: Laser room safety and governance
objectives: Build a pre-use hazard check addressing laser class, controlled area, wavelength-specific eye protection, plume/fire risk, skin prep, equipment checks and emergency roles.
Distinguish FDA product controls from local clinician/operator duties; identify when institutional laser-safety officer review is needed.
units.boardMappingNote: Educational alignment to broad general dermatology knowledge/procedural-safety domains only; no laser/cosmetic board blueprint or board examination is asserted.
units.casePractice: Audit a fictional room setup with an invisible near-infrared class IV beam; flag eyewear and fire/plume deficiencies without operating a device.
units.assessment: Checklist rubric: wavelength-compatible eyewear, controlled area/access, plume/fire, staff roles and incident plan, 4 points each.

units.title: Consultation, diagnosis, candidacy and consent
objectives: Structure a cosmetic consultation around patient goals, medical history, skin examination, alternatives, costs, realistic outcomes and time for informed choice.
Separate diagnosis of a pigmented lesion from elective cosmetic treatment; identify red flags requiring diagnostic workup/referral.
topics: Patient care; communication; ethics and professionalism
boardDomains: Patient care; communication; ethics and professionalism
units.boardMappingNote: Educational alignment to broad general dermatology knowledge/procedural-safety domains only; no laser/cosmetic board blueprint or board examination is asserted.
units.casePractice: Write an informed-consent conversation for a fictional person with an indeterminate changing pigmented lesion requesting laser removal; defer cosmetic destruction until diagnosis is addressed.
units.assessment: OSCE-style rubric: diagnostic safety, elicited expectations, alternatives/risks, teach-back and follow-up; 4 points each.

units.title: Skin phototypes, skin of colour and risk adaptation
objectives: Explain epidermal melanin as a competing chromophore and how post-inflammatory pigment risk affects treatment selection and counselling.
Compare relative rationale and limits of longer-wavelength devices and cooling; do not infer a universally safe parameter or protocol from phototype alone.
topics: Skin of colour; laser safety; patient-centred care
boardDomains: Skin of colour; laser safety; patient-centred care
units.boardMappingNote: Educational alignment to broad general dermatology knowledge/procedural-safety domains only; no laser/cosmetic board blueprint or board examination is asserted.
units.casePractice: Use an authentic, linked DermNet image/case of post-laser pigmentation as a pattern-recognition discussion; do not use it as a parameter recipe.
units.assessment: Case memo: risk mechanism, differential, prevention/monitoring, uncertainty and communication; 5 criteria scored 0–2.

units.title: Vascular lesions and erythema
objectives: Differentiate common vascular cosmetic concerns (telangiectasia/erythema) from mimics and identify when medical evaluation is required.
Relate hemoglobin targeting and pulse concepts to a high-level discussion of vascular devices and adverse effects.
topics: Inflammatory/vascular disease; cutaneous optics; procedural complications
boardDomains: Inflammatory/vascular disease; cutaneous optics; procedural complications
units.boardMappingNote: Educational alignment to broad general dermatology knowledge/procedural-safety domains only; no laser/cosmetic board blueprint or board examination is asserted.
units.casePractice: Compare a fictional facial telangiectasia vignette with persistent inflammatory erythema; outline diagnostic questions and non-prescriptive treatment rationale.
units.assessment: Grading: differential, target rationale, skin/context risks, referral/alternatives; 25% each.

units.title: Pigmentary disorders, melasma and lentigines
objectives: Distinguish melasma, lentigo, post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation and suspicious melanocytic lesions before considering device-based therapy.
Explain why inflammation/thermal injury may aggravate dyschromia and why photoprotection and maintenance planning matter.
topics: Pigmentary disease; skin-of-colour dermatology; laser safety
boardDomains: Pigmentary disease; skin-of-colour dermatology; laser safety
units.boardMappingNote: Educational alignment to broad general dermatology knowledge/procedural-safety domains only; no laser/cosmetic board blueprint or board examination is asserted.
units.casePractice: Analyze the free public webinar chapter on melasma/pigmentation; critique sponsored device claims against an independent reading.
units.assessment: Evidence critique scored 0–4 each: diagnosis, source quality/bias, patient selection, risk/counselling and appropriately qualified conclusion.

units.title: Hair reduction and follicular indications
objectives: Explain the relationship of hair pigment/growth cycle and treatment goals; counsel that efficacy and treatment course vary.
Recognize risks including burns, dyspigmentation, scarring and need for clinician expertise and aftercare.
topics: Hair and follicular disorders; procedural dermatology; patient safety
boardDomains: Hair and follicular disorders; procedural dermatology; patient safety
units.boardMappingNote: Educational alignment to broad general dermatology knowledge/procedural-safety domains only; no laser/cosmetic board blueprint or board examination is asserted.
units.casePractice: Use the AAD safety page to build a counseling checklist; include darker skin and paradoxical/variable response as discussion prompts without promising outcomes.
units.assessment: Checklist rubric: candidacy limits, alternatives, risks, course uncertainty, sun protection and follow-up, 0–2 each.

units.title: Tattoo and exogenous pigment
objectives: Identify tattoo ink colour/depth and patient characteristics as variables; discuss wavelength selection conceptually, not as a treatment prescription.
Explain risks of incomplete clearance, pigment alteration, paradoxical darkening and scarring, and counsel uncertainty.
topics: Pigmentary disorders; device physics; procedural risk
boardDomains: Pigmentary disorders; device physics; procedural risk
units.boardMappingNote: Educational alignment to broad general dermatology knowledge/procedural-safety domains only; no laser/cosmetic board blueprint or board examination is asserted.
units.casePractice: Compare two fictional tattoo consultation scenarios; do not infer ink composition or guarantee clearance from colour alone.
units.assessment: Decision note scored on uncertainty, differential/ink history, risk communication, alternatives and referral criteria.

units.title: Resurfacing, photoaging and scars
objectives: Compare ablative and non-ablative/fractional concepts, healing burden and risk at a mechanism level.
Distinguish cosmetic scar-remodeling goals from active inflammatory disease or suspicious lesions.
topics: Cutaneous surgery; wound healing; photoaging; adverse-event management

units.title: Non-laser energy-based modalities and combination plans
objectives: Recognize that IPL is not a laser and RF/ultrasound mechanisms differ; avoid treating device categories as interchangeable.

objectives: Critique endpoints, follow-up, comparator, selection bias, conflicts and patient-reported outcomes in device studies and marketing.
Design a small QI audit for adverse-event capture and equitable access without inventing expected outcomes or case volumes.

deliverables: A 2-page consultation/candidacy memo for two fictional cases, one with a pigmented lesion and one seeking hair reduction.
A laser-room hazard checklist using FDA class/risks and local policy; it is an audit exercise, not operational authorization.
A one-page comparative evidence critique of an openly viewable webinar with sponsor/conflict disclosure.
A 5-minute oral case defence: diagnosis/differential, risks, alternatives, uncertainty, referral and follow-up.

rubric.criterion: Diagnostic reasoning and differential before cosmetic intervention
Safety, hazard controls and appropriate escalation
Consent, realistic expectations and scope limits

practiceQuestions.stem: Which statement best describes selective photothermolysis?

options.text: Matching an absorbed wavelength and pulse duration to a target while limiting adjacent thermal injury.
Using any continuous beam at maximum energy.
Applying infrared light only to skin with low melanin.
A synonym for FDA clearance.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Selective photothermolysis is a conceptual framework linking target absorption and thermal relaxation; it does not itself specify safe parameters for an individual.

practiceQuestions.stem: A laser-room audit identifies a class IV skin treatment device. Which safety conclusion is best supported by FDA hazard classification?

options.text: Only direct beam exposure can harm.
Direct and reflected exposure can injure eyes/skin and fire risk may exist; institute controls and wavelength-appropriate eyewear are needed.
Class IV automatically means the operator has board certification.
Patient goggles alone control all hazards.

practiceQuestions.rationale: FDA identifies class IV as immediate skin and eye hazard from direct or reflected exposure and possible fire hazard. Product class does not certify operators.

practiceQuestions.stem: A patient with a changing irregular pigmented lesion asks to have it lasered as a sunspot. What is the safest next step?

options.text: Treat with a low setting to preserve diagnostic appearance.
Establish appropriate diagnosis/workup before elective destruction; discuss referral/biopsy as clinically indicated.
Proceed if the patient signs consent.
Select a wavelength based on cosmetic preference.

practiceQuestions.rationale: A suspicious evolving lesion requires diagnostic evaluation; destructive cosmetic treatment can obscure diagnosis. This fictional scenario does not give an individual diagnosis.

practiceQuestions.stem: What is a key laser consideration in Fitzpatrick V–VI skin?

options.text: Melanin is not a relevant chromophore at therapeutic wavelengths.
Competing epidermal melanin can increase unwanted absorption and pigmentary injury risk; individualized assessment and conservative safety planning matter.
A test spot guarantees no delayed dyspigmentation.
A particular wavelength is universally safe for all patients.

practiceQuestions.rationale: DermNet discusses epidermal melanin as competing chromophore and increased risk of PIH; no single universal protocol is implied.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which hair-removal statement is consistent with AAD public education?

options.text: One treatment eliminates all hair permanently in every patient.
Results and course vary; burns, pigment change and scars can occur, and experienced medical supervision and sun/aftercare are important.
Protective eyewear is optional if the patient closes their eyes.
Treatment interval is the same for every individual.

practiceQuestions.rationale: AAD lists variability, treatment sessions, risks and importance of skilled clinicians and eye protection; avoid guarantees.

practiceQuestions.stem: Why does melasma require caution when considering device-based pigment treatment?

options.text: Any response to a laser proves a diagnosis of melasma.
Inflammation/thermal injury can worsen dyschromia; confirm diagnosis, weigh alternatives and counsel recurrence/uncertainty rather than promise clearance.
Melasma is always a benign lentigo.
Only the color of the spot matters.

practiceQuestions.rationale: This answer reflects pigmentary risk and clinical diagnosis; video content is an educational resource, not a treatment protocol.

practiceQuestions.stem: What is the best way to use a commercial free webinar in a curriculum?

options.text: Treat it as an unbiased guideline because it is publicly hosted.
Note its sponsor, extract supported educational points, and cross-check claims with independent evidence.
Rehost the video and transcript in the course without asking.
Count all adjacent playlist items as watched lecture hours.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The free pigmentation webinar page explicitly discloses sponsorship; open access does not remove bias or copyright concerns.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which statement about board status is most accurate for a laser/cosmetic dermatology fellowship?

options.text: Completing it grants a separate ABD laser board certificate.
ABD separately lists exams/eligibility for named subspecialties; this laser fellowship page does not claim a distinct board exam or eligibility, so confirm status with ABD and the program.
Any institutional fellowship automatically creates board eligibility.
Licensure and board certification are interchangeable.

practiceQuestions.rationale: ABD lists dermatopathology, micrographic dermatologic surgery and pediatric dermatology subspecialty certification prerequisites, while the MGB page describes a fellowship and no laser exam. Do not infer eligibility.

practiceQuestions.stem: A changing suspicious pigmented lesion is being evaluated. Which strategy best preserves diagnostic microstaging when feasible?

options.text: Cauterize and record clinical diameter
Biopsy that permits histopathologic assessment of the lesion and depth; local excision is preferred when feasible
Dermoscopy alone and wait six months
Intentionally transect the base with a superficial shave

practiceQuestions.rationale: NCI recommends biopsy, preferably local excision where feasible, and warns against destructive sampling that prevents microstaging. Feasibility and technique are clinician-dependent; this is not procedure training.

practiceQuestions.stem: A cutaneous melanoma is 0.9 mm thick without ulceration. Under AJCC 8, which T1 category applies?

options.text: T1a, because all lesions under 1 mm are T1a
T1b: 0.8–1.0 mm, with or without ulceration
T2a, because ≥0.8 mm is T2
No category without mitotic rate

practiceQuestions.rationale: AJCC 8 defines T1b as 0.8–1.0 mm with or without ulceration. Mitotic rate is reported but is not a T1 category criterion in AJCC 8. Verify the edition in current use.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which statement about an evolving lesion without visible brown pigment is most accurate?

options.text: Lack of pigment excludes melanoma
Amelanotic melanoma is possible; evolution and context remain important
Dermoscopy alone proves benignity
Only lesions >6 mm warrant evaluation

practiceQuestions.rationale: Melanoma can be amelanotic; size or color alone cannot exclude it. Histology is used for suspicious lesions.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which pathology data elements are central to AJCC T classification of invasive cutaneous melanoma?

options.text: Color score only
Breslow thickness and ulceration status
Patient-reported lesion duration only
Clark level alone

practiceQuestions.rationale: Thickness and ulceration are central T elements; other elements such as margins and mitotic rate remain important in report interpretation.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which best characterizes sentinel lymph node biopsy (SLNB) in melanoma?

options.text: Therapeutic removal of all regional nodes in every patient
Staging/prognostic procedure considered for selected patients after individualized discussion
Indicated for all melanoma in situ
Negative result proves zero future metastatic risk

practiceQuestions.rationale: SLNB is a staging procedure discussed for appropriate patients; not for melanoma in situ, and a negative result does not eliminate future risk.

practiceQuestions.stem: For lentigo maligna at a constrained facial site, what is the best approach to a Mohs/staged excision question?

options.text: Universal first-line for every invasive melanoma
Review selected melanoma-in-situ/lentigo-maligna margin-control guidance and local expertise; involve appropriate specialists
Avoid histologic margin assessment
Assume the visible pigmented border is the tumor margin

practiceQuestions.rationale: AAD notes staged excision/Mohs can provide exhaustive peripheral margin assessment for selected melanoma in situ, lentigo maligna type. It is not universal treatment for invasive melanoma.

practiceQuestions.stem: A tumor test shows BRAF V600 alteration in advanced melanoma. What conclusion is most appropriate?

options.text: Permanent response to BRAF monotherapy is guaranteed
May inform treatment selection in the right setting; assess current indications, resistance, alternatives and risks
It proves a germline inherited syndrome
It eliminates immunotherapy or trials

practiceQuestions.rationale: Somatic tumor findings may inform targeted options but do not prove inherited risk or guarantee response. NCI notes combination BRAF/MEK therapy and resistance.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which statement distinguishes hereditary-risk evaluation from tumor testing?

options.text: A tumor BRAF variant proves germline syndrome
Germline tests evaluate inherited variants; tumor testing detects somatic changes and may guide treatment
Family history is irrelevant when tumor sequencing is done
Every melanoma requires broad germline testing

practiceQuestions.rationale: Germline and somatic tests answer distinct questions; testing is risk/pedigree-dependent and benefits from genetic counseling.

practiceQuestions.stem: As of 2026-10-07, which best describes the FDA’s 2026 accelerated approval of vusolimogene oderparepvec-wtpg?

options.text: A cure for all melanoma stages
With nivolumab for adults with unresectable advanced cutaneous melanoma progressing after a PD-1 regimen; accelerated approval requires confirmation
Standard neoadjuvant therapy for all stage II melanoma
No infection-related warnings

practiceQuestions.rationale: FDA approval (2026-08-06) was limited to adults with unresectable advanced cutaneous melanoma after PD-1 progression, under accelerated approval requiring post-approval confirmation; infection-related warnings are stated. Recheck current label.

practiceQuestions.stem: An educator uses an ISIC Archive image in a slide. What is the appropriate rights approach?

options.text: Public access means all images are public domain
Check item/collection-specific license, provenance, privacy and terms; link rather than repost unless reuse is expressly permitted
Labels always verify diagnosis
Credit alone permits commercial reuse

practiceQuestions.rationale: Public access is not blanket reuse permission. Check terms, image provenance, annotations, license and privacy restrictions. This course does not copy images.

title: Dermatology/Rheumatology Fellowship
level: Clinical physician fellowship (institutional advanced-training track; not a combined board-certification residency)-aligned independent study

prerequisites.level: Advanced physician self-study for dermatology trainees, dermatologists, and rheumatology clinicians seeking structured cross-specialty knowledge; not an entry-level clinical credential.
recommended: Medical-school-level immunology, pathology, pharmacology, and clinical reasoning.
Prior dermatology training or supervised dermatology practice for the intended fellowship-facing level; internal-medicine/rheumatology background is useful for systemic-organ assessment.
Ability to interpret basic CBC, metabolic panel, urinalysis, inflammatory markers, autoantibodies, muscle enzymes, skin histopathology reports, and pulmonary-function data with supervision.
Familiarity with shared decision-making, medication safety, and urgent escalation for organ-threatening disease.
prerequisites.institutionalEligibility: The programme's public page directs applicants to contact BWH Dermatology for details; exact eligibility prerequisites are not published on the reviewed page. Do not infer eligibility from this course.

objectives: Describe morphology and distribution of cutaneous connective-tissue disease manifestations while retaining a broad differential and considering skin phototype, mimics, and medication effects.
Distinguish cutaneous lupus subtypes and reason about when skin findings warrant evaluation for systemic disease without equating classification criteria with diagnosis.
Integrate skin, muscle, lung, vascular, renal, and joint findings in dermatomyositis, systemic sclerosis, vasculitis, and overlap syndromes.

Select and interpret appropriate investigations, including biopsy with clinicopathologic correlation, serology, urinalysis, muscle enzymes, pulmonary function tests, and imaging, recognizing test limitations.
Summarize guideline-informed treatment classes and safety monitoring, applying patient-specific factors and shared decision-making rather than memorized treatment orders.
Communicate uncertainty and coordinate dermatology-rheumatology care, referrals, urgent red flags, and evidence-informed follow-up.

Use board-style clinical vignettes for diagnostic reasoning while distinguishing ABIM rheumatology domains from ABD dermatology certification content and the absence of a dedicated rheumatic-dermatology board exam.

units.title: Visual language, morphology, and the cross-specialty examination
objectives: Describe primary and secondary lesions, distribution, configuration, mucosa, scalp, nails, and vascular findings precisely.
Build a differential before using a disease label and identify when urgent systemic assessment is needed.
topics: Morphology and distribution; skin phototypes and dyspigmentation; history of onset, photosensitivity, medication exposure, systemic symptoms; review of systems; standardized photography and consent.
boardDomains: ABD: clinical dermatology and diagnostic reasoning (broad mapping; consult current ABD content overview)
ABIM Rheumatology: clinical assessment and differential diagnosis (broad mapping; consult current ABIM blueprint)
units.casePractice: Use linked DermNet rheumatic-skin image pages for morphology-only descriptions; no image is downloaded or rehosted.
units.assessment: Submit a one-page lesion description and differential for two selected images; rubric: morphology 40%, differential 30%, systemic red flags 20%, uncertainty/communication 10%.

units.title: Cutaneous lupus: classification, biopsy, and systemic context
objectives: Compare acute, subacute, and chronic cutaneous lupus morphology and scarring risk.
Use clinicopathologic correlation and systemic history to decide what further evaluation to discuss with a supervisor.
topics: ACLE, SCLE, DLE, tumid and chilblain lupus; photosensitivity; scarring alopecia; drug-induced CLE; biopsy/serology limits; classification versus diagnosis.
boardDomains: ABIM Rheumatology: SLE manifestations and diagnostic evaluation
units.casePractice: Compare linked DermNet CLE examples; practice describing morphology, distribution, scarring, and uncertainty without making a diagnosis from an image alone.
units.assessment: Construct a morphology-to-differential table for four fictional image descriptions; rubric: subtype reasoning 35%, competing diagnoses 25%, systemic evaluation considerations 25%, source use 15%.

units.title: SLE with skin disease: activity, organ screening, and treatment reasoning
objectives: Separate cutaneous activity from systemic activity and identify organ-threatening features.
Summarize current guideline recommendations and safety qualifiers for major treatment classes.
topics: Skin and mucosal disease; renal/hematologic/neurologic review; urinalysis/protein quantification; hydroxychloroquine target-dose principle and retinal-risk monitoring; glucocorticoid minimization; guideline-directed immunomodulation; pregnancy and comorbidity considerations.
boardDomains: ABIM Rheumatology: SLE diagnosis, disease manifestations, treatment and complications
ABD: cutaneous lupus diagnosis and management
units.casePractice: Fictional case: photosensitive eruption plus new proteinuria. Practice identifying the need for timely systemic assessment; no treatment order or real-patient advice.
units.assessment: Write a structured problem representation and a guideline source map; rubric: disease synthesis 30%, safety/urgency 30%, guideline accuracy 25%, uncertainty 15%.

units.title: Dermatomyositis and inflammatory myopathy with skin findings
objectives: Distinguish characteristic skin findings from mimics and avoid diagnosing myositis from rash alone.
Integrate muscle, lung, swallowing, and malignancy-risk assessment using validated guidance.
topics: Gottron papules/sign, heliotrope eruption, shawl/V-sign, mechanic's hands, nailfold changes; muscle weakness and enzymes; myositis antibodies; ILD assessment; cancer-risk stratification; amyopathic/hypomyopathic presentations; mimics.
boardDomains: ABIM Rheumatology: inflammatory myopathy and systemic complications
ABD: inflammatory and connective-tissue skin disease
units.casePractice: Use DermNet educational dermatomyositis images as authentic linked examples subject to the image licence; pair with a fictional weakness/dyspnea vignette.
units.assessment: Submit a diagnostic reasoning matrix separating skin, muscle, lung, swallowing, and malignancy domains; rubric: domain coverage 40%, appropriate tests 25%, red flags 20%, limits 15%.

units.title: Systemic sclerosis and scleroderma-spectrum skin disease
objectives: Recognize sclerodactyly, digital ulcers, telangiectasia, Raynaud phenomena, and mimics.
Connect cutaneous phenotype with cardiopulmonary, renal, gastrointestinal and vascular risk without overcalling limited or diffuse subtype.
topics: Raynaud assessment; nailfold capillaroscopy concepts; skin thickening; morphea vs systemic sclerosis; autoantibodies as context; ILD, pulmonary hypertension, renal crisis and GI screening; patient-centered symptom burden.
boardDomains: ABIM Rheumatology: systemic sclerosis and organ complications
units.casePractice: Compare DermNet-linked systemic sclerosis and morphea images; explicitly note that clinical images alone cannot stage systemic disease.
units.assessment: Draft a cross-specialty consultation checklist; rubric: skin characterization 25%, organ-screening concepts 35%, differential 20%, communication 20%.

units.title: Cutaneous vasculitis, vascular occlusion, and systemic danger signs
objectives: Differentiate palpable purpura, livedo, retiform purpura, ulcers, and vasculopathic mimics.
Identify renal, pulmonary, neurologic, gastrointestinal, ischemic, infectious, and medication-related red flags.
topics: Vessel-size patterns; timing and site of biopsy; direct immunofluorescence considerations; CBC, renal function, urinalysis, complement and targeted serology; AAV/GCA/IgA and other causes; urgent referral principles.
boardDomains: ABIM Rheumatology: vasculitis classification, diagnostic workup and management
units.casePractice: Use linked educational images for pattern recognition and a fictional palpable-purpura case; never infer systemic vasculitis from skin appearance alone.
units.assessment: Create an escalation flowchart for a fictional case; rubric: life-threatening features 35%, differential 25%, test selection 25%, safety language 15%.

units.title: Psoriasis, psoriatic arthritis, and other inflammatory overlap
objectives: Characterize psoriasis and nail disease while screening for inflammatory musculoskeletal symptoms.
Distinguish common comorbidity and overlap patterns from proof of a particular systemic diagnosis.
topics: Plaque/inverse/pustular patterns; nail pitting/onycholysis; inflammatory back pain, enthesitis, dactylitis, peripheral arthritis; treatment class awareness and interdisciplinary referral.
boardDomains: ABIM Rheumatology: inflammatory arthritis and spondyloarthritis
ABD: papulosquamous disease and nail findings
units.casePractice: Use DermNet psoriasis pages as linked learning material and fictional vignettes; do not reproduce photos.
units.assessment: Design five screening questions and explain referral thresholds; rubric: clinically useful questions 40%, differential 25%, limitations 20%, clarity 15%.

units.title: Rheumatoid arthritis and systemic disease clues in skin
objectives: Recognize rheumatoid nodules, vasculitic lesions, neutrophilic dermatoses, and drug-related eruptions as differential categories.
Integrate joint pattern, serology, medication chronology, and infection risk without treating any skin feature as pathognomonic.
topics: Nodules; rheumatoid vasculitis; neutrophilic and ulcerative mimics; DMARD/biologic-related cutaneous adverse events; infection versus flare; referral and biopsy coordination.
boardDomains: ABIM Rheumatology: rheumatoid arthritis and treatment complications
ABD: inflammatory, ulcerative and medication-related dermatoses
units.casePractice: Construct a fictional medication timeline and compare adverse drug reaction, infection, and disease activity hypotheses.
units.assessment: Submit a differential and medication-safety memo; rubric: timeline 30%, plausible alternatives 30%, red flags 25%, source use 15%.

units.title: Overlap syndromes, Sjögren disease, and autoinflammatory clues
objectives: Recognize xerosis, sicca-related findings, chilblain-like lesions, mucosal signs, and overlap phenotypes.
Use history and targeted testing without overinterpreting low-specificity autoantibodies.
topics: Sjögren disease; mixed connective tissue disease; overlap myositis; relapsing polychondritis; autoinflammatory patterns; test pretest probability and false positives.
boardDomains: ABIM Rheumatology: systemic autoimmune and autoinflammatory disease
units.casePractice: Use linked public skin-sign descriptions; practice stating what additional history/examination would change the differential.
units.assessment: Produce a one-page uncertainty-aware consult note; rubric: synthesis 35%, test interpretation 25%, differential 25%, communication 15%.

units.title: Biopsy, serology, imaging, and clinicopathologic correlation
objectives: Choose a biopsy site and test strategy based on morphology, age of lesion, and suspected process.
Explain why histology, autoantibodies, and classification criteria must be integrated with clinical findings.
topics: H&E and direct immunofluorescence concepts; specimen handling (confirm local lab protocol); ANA/ENA/myositis panels; sensitivity, specificity, pretest probability; lung function and imaging concepts; avoid indiscriminate testing.
boardDomains: ABD: diagnostic methods and dermatopathology interpretation
ABIM Rheumatology: diagnostic studies and clinical reasoning
units.casePractice: Read selected publicly linked educational case reports and compare the clinical question with limitations of each test; no patient records copied.
units.assessment: For three fictional vignettes, justify one next investigation and one limitation; rubric: indication 35%, interpretation 30%, pretest probability 20%, safe caveats 15%.

units.title: Systemic therapeutics, treatment safety, and shared decisions
objectives: Compare topical, antimalarial, conventional immunomodulatory, biologic, and glucocorticoid roles at a conceptual level.
Identify common safety, monitoring, infection, pregnancy, comorbidity, and ophthalmic considerations requiring current source review.
topics: Guideline-directed SLE care; organ-threat stratification; medication reconciliation; infection/vaccination review; retinal screening with hydroxychloroquine; steroid-sparing principles; adverse event differential; patient priorities.
boardDomains: ABIM Rheumatology: therapeutics, adverse effects and complications
units.casePractice: A fictional shared-decision case compares patient priorities and risk factors; do not write prescriptions or provide individual treatment advice.
units.assessment: Submit a treatment-class comparison matrix citing one current guideline per claim; rubric: source currency 30%, risk/benefit reasoning 35%, monitoring 20%, shared decision-making 15%.

units.title: Integrated case conference, board-style reasoning, and longitudinal care
objectives: Synthesize morphology, systemic features, investigation results, and uncertainty into a concise problem representation.
Prioritize immediate safety issues, referral coordination, monitoring and patient-centered follow-up.
topics: Cross-specialty case conference; longitudinal change; documentation; health equity and skin of color; communication; evidence appraisal; board-style single-best-answer reasoning.

medical.programmeSourceScope: The packet classified this as a clinical physician fellowship. The primary programme page confirms a one-year fellowship aimed at academic dermatologists, with clinical evaluation, systemic therapeutics, multidisciplinary care, elective and translational/clinical research opportunities. It is not merely a research-only postdoctoral appointment or non-physician supplement. The public page locates it within Dermatology; its description does not state that it is a combined dermatology and internal-medicine residency, an ACGME-accredited rheumatology fellowship, or a two-board pathway. The RDS listing confirms a Brigham/Harvard institutional name variant. The independent curriculum supplements study only and does not replicate the programme's supervised clinical experience.
sourceCaveats: Programme page and directory listing prove public listing and published description only. The detailed curriculum, complete eligibility criteria, accreditation status, didactic contact hours, fellow outcomes, and any institutional board eligibility assurance were not publicly established in this review.

The programme is described as year-long and aimed at academic dermatologists; it should not be represented as a combined specialty residency, ABIM-accredited rheumatology fellowship, or dual-board pathway.

The ABIM rheumatology examination is a distinct, real certification exam. The fellowship itself publishes no dedicated board examination. ABD certification is a separate dermatology board pathway; no dedicated rheumatic dermatology certification was identified in reviewed public sources.

ABIM's official PDF was linked and recognized as its blueprint, but extraction was corrupted by the PDF fetcher. The curriculum therefore uses broad clinical reasoning alignment and does not claim a precise percentage-by-topic mapping.
EULAR/ACR recommendations are date-sensitive; this curriculum was checked 2026-10-07. Use current full guideline documents and local protocols before clinical application.
Human clinical review is not performed. No diagnosis, treatment order, eligibility determination, clinical case volume, or guarantee of board success is provided.

Eighteen candidate links have unknown runtime; none is counted. The 26 original clip plans collectively target 2,190 minutes (36.5 h) of future production, not ready video and not included in hours.

practiceQuestions.stem: A learner is given an educational photo of a chronic, scaly, well-demarcated plaque with follicular plugging and central atrophy on sun-exposed skin. Which description best captures the key diagnostic concern while preserving appropriate uncertainty?

options.text: The image proves systemic lupus erythematosus.
The morphology is compatible with chronic cutaneous/discoid lupus; clinicopathologic and systemic context are still needed.
This is diagnostic of dermatomyositis.
A single ANA result is sufficient to classify the eruption.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Discoid lesions can scar and involve follicles, but images alone do not establish systemic lupus; clinical history, examination, and sometimes biopsy or other evaluation are needed.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which feature most strongly raises concern for irreversible cutaneous damage in chronic discoid lupus compared with typical subacute cutaneous lupus?

options.text: A non-scarring photosensitive papulosquamous eruption.
Follicular involvement with atrophy and scarring alopecia.
Transient flushing without scale.
Isolated nail pitting.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Chronic discoid lesions may cause atrophy, dyspigmentation, and scarring alopecia; SCLE is often photosensitive but typically does not scar.

practiceQuestions.stem: A question asks which EULAR 2023 recommendation is stated for hydroxychloroquine in SLE. Which response is most accurate?

options.text: Use the same dose for every patient and omit eye-risk review.
For most patients unless contraindicated, a target of 5 mg/kg/day real body weight is recommended, individualized for flare and retinal-toxicity risk.
Avoid hydroxychloroquine in all patients with cutaneous manifestations.
Use it only after irreversible renal failure.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The EULAR recommendation includes a target dose based on real body weight and individualization; this is guideline learning, not a prescription for an individual.

practiceQuestions.stem: A fictional adult has a new dermatomyositis-compatible eruption, proximal weakness, and dyspnea. Which learning response is best?

options.text: Treat the eruption as proof that malignancy is present.
Consider myositis and pulmonary involvement, assess urgently in clinical care, and apply current risk-stratified evaluation guidance rather than blanket screening.
Reassure because skin findings exclude lung disease.
Use classification criteria alone to diagnose and prescribe.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Dermatomyositis may involve muscle and lung and carries age/phenotype-dependent cancer risk; IMACS guidance supports risk stratification. Dyspnea and weakness need real clinical assessment.
practiceQuestions.domain: Inflammatory myopathy, organ risk, malignancy screening

practiceQuestions.stem: A fictional patient with palpable purpura also has new hematuria and rising creatinine. What is the most defensible next educational conclusion?

options.text: This is a skin-limited process because lesions are palpable.
Potential systemic small-vessel disease with kidney involvement must be considered; prompt clinical evaluation is needed and skin appearance alone is insufficient.
A positive ANCA, if found, would prove one specific vasculitis.
No further assessment is indicated if the rash fades.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Purpura with renal findings can indicate systemic disease and warrants timely evaluation. ANCA results require clinical context and differential diagnosis.
practiceQuestions.domain: Vasculitis red flags and systemic workup

practiceQuestions.stem: Which statement best distinguishes systemic sclerosis from localized morphea for educational differential reasoning?

options.text: Any sclerotic plaque establishes systemic sclerosis.
Skin thickening patterns need contextual assessment; morphea is localized, while systemic sclerosis requires assessment for vascular and internal-organ features.
Raynaud phenomenon is never relevant.
A skin photograph can stage lung disease.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Clinical phenotype, vascular findings, history, investigations, and organ assessment distinguish sclerosing disorders; images alone cannot stage systemic disease.
practiceQuestions.domain: Systemic sclerosis differential and organ context

practiceQuestions.stem: A fictional patient with psoriasis reports prolonged morning stiffness, a swollen digit, and heel pain. What is the best next reasoning step?

options.text: Assume the symptoms are mechanical because psoriasis is cutaneous.
Elicit a focused inflammatory musculoskeletal history and arrange appropriate rheumatologic assessment; skin disease alone does not prove psoriatic arthritis.
Diagnose psoriatic arthritis from nail pitting alone.
Order every autoantibody panel without regard to pretest probability.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Inflammatory stiffness, dactylitis, and enthesitis are relevant clues that merit focused assessment, but no single skin or nail feature alone establishes the arthritis diagnosis.

practiceQuestions.stem: A patient has a low-positive autoantibody but no compatible symptoms or examination findings. Which interpretation is most appropriate?

options.text: The test alone confirms systemic autoimmune disease.
Interpret the result with pretest probability, assay limitations, and the full clinical picture; avoid diagnosis by isolated serology.
Repeat the same test weekly until positive at a higher titre.
Ignore any future systemic symptoms because the test is already known.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Autoantibodies are interpreted in context; indiscriminate testing may produce misleading positives and classification does not replace clinical diagnosis.
practiceQuestions.domain: Diagnostic test interpretation and pretest probability

practiceQuestions.stem: A course designer wants to use a DermNet watermarked clinical image in a noncommercial student slide deck. Which use best follows the published image terms?

options.text: Remove the watermark and crop it into a new composite.
Use the watermarked image with clear DermNet attribution and active source link, preserve it unmodified, and do not redistribute a derivative or use it commercially.
Assume public viewing means unrestricted commercial reuse.
Upload the image to an AI training dataset.

practiceQuestions.rationale: DermNet's free educational image terms specify attribution and link, noncommercial use, no distributed derivatives, retained watermark, and prohibit AI training use of free images.

practiceQuestions.stem: A physician asks whether completing the BWH Dermatology/Rheumatology Fellowship itself qualifies them for the ABIM Rheumatology board examination. Which answer is best supported by the public sources?

options.text: Yes, any fellowship with rheumatology in its name grants ABIM eligibility.
No such eligibility is established by the public programme page; ABIM eligibility is a separate board-defined pathway, and ACGME Rheumatology requirements specify distinct prerequisites.
The programme awards a combined ABD-ABIM certificate.
There is a dedicated rheumatic-dermatology board exam administered by the fellowship.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The official BWH/MGB page describes a year-long fellowship for academic dermatologists; ABIM separately publishes its certification pathway and ACGME separately states accredited rheumatology fellowship requirements. No rheumatic-dermatology-specific board exam was identified in the reviewed public materials.
