assignment.title: Longitudinal fictional perioperative pathway portfolio
assignment.instructions: For one composite, explicitly fictional adult elective-surgery case, produce (1) consult note with missing information separated from assumptions; (2) risk and selective-testing rationale; (3) optimization, medication and shared-decision plan with dated references; (4) ambulatory/inpatient setting and escalation analysis; (5) structured handoff/discharge plan; and (6) one QI aim with outcome, process and balancing measures. Do not use patient records, identifiable data or copied case narratives. Tool calculations, if any, must use synthetic values and honor source terms.

rubric.risk_reasoning: 25% — identifies urgency, key conditions, risk modifiers and limits of estimates.
rubric.evidence: 20% — selects current authoritative guidance, quotes scope/date and distinguishes recommendation from local policy.
rubric.patient/team communication: 20% — communicates uncertainty, goals, consultation ownership and shared choices.
rubric.setting/recovery/safety: 20% — includes facility capability, handoff, monitoring, discharge and transfer contingencies.
rubric.QI/equity/ethics: 15% — proposes measurable improvement with balancing measure and appropriate privacy/equity safeguards.

assignment.passingInterpretation: Course-design formative standard only; not validated, not a board score, and not evidence of clinical competence.

components: 12 unit formative knowledge checks (one per unit)
end-of-course oral defense of one fictional pathway
assessment.masteryRule: Suggested educational threshold 80% on formative quiz plus satisfactory completion of portfolio; repeat learning after errors. This suggested threshold is not an official board pass standard or predictor.
assessment.limitations: Questions are original and educational, not official ABA exam questions, validated psychometrics, a board predictor or patient-care authorization.

studyHours.plan: Suggested 108 hours of self-study across 12 units: 5 hours source reading, 2 hours video viewing when verified media become available, 1 hour case/assessment and 1 hour synthesis per unit. Separate from the planned 36 production video-hours. This is a learner workload plan, not BWH fellowship time or measured learning time.
studyHours.countingNote: No planned film, written script, reading, podcast, podcast runtime, institutional rotation or case exercise is counted as a ready lecture-video hour.

unitMap.text: Perioperative medicine as a system and consultant practice
coveredTopics: Scope and transitions; shared decision-making; consultation triage; care pathways; value and access.

unitMap.text: Preanesthesia consultation, risk framing and selective testing
coveredTopics: ASA status and limits; record review; focused exam; test selection; consent; NICE scope and differences.

unitMap.text: Cardiovascular risk and perioperative decisions
coveredTopics: 2024 AHA/ACC stepwise approach; RCRI/NSQIP; DASI; frailty; BNP/NT-proBNP/troponin; CAD, HF, valve disease, arrhythmia, devices; antithrombotic issues.

unitMap.text: Pulmonary disease, OSA, airway and noncardiac comorbidity
coveredTopics: COPD/asthma; smoking cessation; OSA; pulmonary hypertension; respiratory reserve; aspiration; NORA environmental risk.

unitMap.text: Medication reconciliation, fasting, diabetes and GLP-1 agents
coveredTopics: Medication reconciliation; diabetes/metabolic disease; aspiration; fasting; GLP-1 escalation, GI symptoms, diet, ultrasound as context-specific option.

unitMap.text: Older adults, frailty, cognition, goals and equity
coveredTopics: Geriatric assessment; frailty; cognition; delirium; advance care planning; social determinants; accessibility and bias.

unitMap.text: Anemia, blood management and transfusion strategy
coveredTopics: Screening/iron status; inflammation/renal disease; blood conservation; consent; transfusion; bleeding/thrombosis coordination.

unitMap.text: Enhanced recovery, prehabilitation, analgesia and recovery goals
coveredTopics: ERAS principles; prehabilitation; multimodal analgesia; opioid stewardship; fluid/temperature/nausea considerations; implementation fidelity.

unitMap.text: Ambulatory anesthesia, NORA and selecting the right setting
coveredTopics: Patient/procedure selection; office/ASC/hospital capabilities; airway/rescue; NORA; discharge; transfer; follow-up; continuous regional catheter considerations.

unitMap.text: Postanesthesia care, complications and handoffs
coveredTopics: PACU; oxygenation/ventilation/circulation/consciousness/temperature; analgesia/nausea; handoffs; unplanned admission; follow-up.

unitMap.text: Quality, safety, operations, leadership and implementation
coveredTopics: Incident learning; event review; just culture; Lean/QI; OR management; capacity; staffing; patient flow; safety culture; value.

unitMap.text: Ethics, evidence, research and scholarly communication
coveredTopics: Shared decisions; capacity; perioperative DNR conversation; conflicts; research design; data governance; outcomes and equity; evidence updating.

boardNames: American Board of Anesthesiology (ABA) initial certification pathway: BASIC, ADVANCED, APPLIED (SOE/OSCE); in-training exam is a programme assessment, not a specialty board.

No separate ABA Perioperative Medicine board/subspecialty certification or dedicated examination identified as of 2026-10-07. ABA announced a perioperative-medicine content-outline topic, with related exam questions beginning in 2028.
medical.boardStatus: This BWH-named physician fellowship is a programme title, not a distinct ABA board. The ABA lists its initial anesthesiology examinations (BASIC, ADVANCED, APPLIED) and subspecialty exams. ABA and ASA announced on 2026-07-22 that perioperative medicine is a newly defined clinical topic within the initial-certification content outline; related new exam questions are scheduled to appear beginning in 2028. No separate Perioperative Medicine board examination/certification was identified in the reviewed ABA material as of 2026-10-07.
medical.boardEligibilityNotice: Completion of this independent course does not confer eligibility for ABA initial certification or an ABA subspecialty exam. Eligibility must be verified directly against current ABA requirements and the relevant accredited training pathway. The BWH webpage publicly describes a 12-month fellowship with attending anesthesiologist clinical work and administrative, research and didactic components; the webpage does not establish ACGME accreditation or a separate board eligibility pathway.

officialProgrammes.name: BWH Perioperative Medicine Fellowship
officialProgrammes.publicCurriculumNotes: Official page describes 12-month full-time experience; four major components: administrative rotations, didactics, projects/research and clinical work as staff/attending anesthesiologist. Named rotations include preoperative evaluation, OR management, perioperative hospital services, QI/safety, NORA, geriatrics, Ariadne Labs, pain leadership, palliative medicine, hospital leadership, perioperative nursing/procedural areas, innovation and ethics. Page states attending anesthesiologist work 0.4 FTE, rotations 0.4 FTE, research 0.2 FTE. This is the public programme page, not a publicly complete lecture syllabus or accreditation proof.

medical.programmeSourceScope: Exact BWH official variant only. Source was followed and read. The BWH programme is explicitly a clinical physician fellowship, not a generic directory category or research-only/non-physician supplement; its page describes attending anesthesiologist clinical service, administrative/clinical rotations and research. No combined-programme designation is made on the page. The public page does not provide a full didactic syllabus or document ACGME accreditation. ACGME requirements index covers anesthesiology residency and listed subspecialties; absence of this fellowship from the publicly visible list is not itself proof of non-accreditation. Preserve programme title exactly as institutional variant.
sourceCaveats: ABA exam-topic announcement is dated 2026-07-22. It says the content outline update will inform author assignments and related questions begin in 2028; this is not a new standalone certification.
2024 AHA/ACC guideline and 2024 GLP-1 multi-society guidance should be checked for updates before clinical use; local institutional protocol and patient-specific clinician judgment remain essential.
NICE NG45 is an England/UK guideline for adults over 16 elective surgery; it excludes pregnancy, cardiothoracic surgery and neurosurgery and is not a universal US mandate.

ACS NSQIP calculator returns estimates, not guarantees; tool prohibits automated integration and should only be opened/used in its original form; no identifiable patient details are used in this curriculum.
AHRQ WebM&M stories are reported/anonymized educational case narratives and are assigned as linked readings only. No case images or record data copied.

medical.sourceReviewNote: Source-cited research and automated checks; not clinician validation or exam-passing prediction.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which statement best describes an appropriate preanesthesia assessment?

options.text: Rely on an old problem list if no symptoms are reported.
Review records, take relevant history, perform focused exam, order pertinent tests as needed, obtain consent, and document.
Order a full panel for every adult before every procedure.
Delegate the anesthetic plan and consent to the surgeon without review.

practiceQuestions.rationale: ASA standards place responsibility on the anesthesiologist to determine status, plan care, review history/record, examine, order pertinent tests and ensure consent. [R10]

practiceQuestions.stem: A stable asymptomatic adult with adequate function is scheduled for a low-risk procedure. What is the best general approach to routine preoperative cardiac stress testing?

options.text: Order it for every patient older than 65.
Order it because surgery creates cardiac stress.
Do not routinely test when low risk, adequate functional capacity/stable symptoms, or low-risk procedure applies.
Test only if ACS is present.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The 2024 guideline reserves stress testing for selected elevated-risk patients with poor/unknown functional capacity when it may inform management; routine testing in low-risk situations is not recommended. [R7]

practiceQuestions.stem: For a patient with known cardiovascular disease and elevated-risk noncardiac surgery, which strategy best reflects the 2024 guideline?

options.text: Use one biomarker as a clearance certificate.
Integrate validated risk estimation, functional capacity and patient-specific factors; order further tests only if results could alter decisions or care.
Perform routine invasive coronary angiography.
Ignore surgical urgency and patient goals.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Guideline emphasizes a stepwise, individualized evaluation; testing should be selected based on risk and expected decision impact; routine invasive angiography is not recommended. [R7]

practiceQuestions.stem: A patient on stable maintenance GLP-1 therapy without relevant GI symptoms is being assessed before elective surgery. Which is most accurate as of the cited multi-society 2024 guidance?

options.text: All patients must stop the drug for a week.
Most patients can continue; higher-risk circumstances call for individualized mitigation/coordination.
GLP-1 therapy never affects aspiration risk.
The anesthesiologist should change diabetes treatment without coordinating.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The 2024 multi-society guidance summary says most patients can continue; escalation, significant GI symptoms, higher dose and delayed gastric emptying conditions trigger individualized mitigation and possible deferral. Recheck for later updates. [R13]

practiceQuestions.stem: Which description of the ACS NSQIP risk estimate is correct?

options.text: A guarantee of outcome.
A complete substitute for clinical judgment.
An estimate based on selected patient/procedure factors that may omit risks and does not guarantee results.
A diagnostic result for cardiovascular disease.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The tool explicitly calls estimates non-guaranteed, based on selected inputs and not a substitute for clinician advice. [R15]

practiceQuestions.stem: What is a defensible use of preoperative testing under NICE NG45?

options.text: Apply every recommendation to children and cardiothoracic surgery.
Select tests by surgery grade and comorbidity within the adult elective scope, noting exclusions and clinical context.
Use tests as universal administrative clearance.
Assume NICE supersedes local policy in every jurisdiction.

practiceQuestions.rationale: NG45 applies to people over 16 undergoing elective surgery; it excludes pregnancy, cardiothoracic procedures and neurosurgery and varies testing with procedure/comorbidities. [R14]

practiceQuestions.stem: For outpatient anesthesia recovery, which handoff/discharge statement best aligns with ASA standards?

options.text: The anesthesiologist has no post-procedure responsibility.
Appropriate postanesthesia care, ongoing evaluation and documented discharge responsibility are required; setting capability and patient status matter.
A single normal oxygen saturation guarantees discharge.
All patients can self-discharge.

practiceQuestions.rationale: ASA postanesthesia and ambulatory statements describe PACU/equivalent care, monitoring, transfer/handoff and physician responsibility for discharge; no single score guarantees outcome. [R11][R12]

practiceQuestions.stem: What is the central systems lesson from AHRQ WebM&M “Haste Makes Care Unsafe”?

options.text: Blame the trainee for every handoff error.
Production pressure and incomplete handoff can align with device hazards; structured communication and safety systems can reduce risk.
PA catheters should always be used.
Handoffs are unnecessary during urgent cases.

practiceQuestions.rationale: AHRQ case/commentary emphasizes production pressure, a missed device-state detail, and structured handoff/checklist systems. [R17]

practiceQuestions.stem: A preoperative CBC shows anemia before an elective major operation. What is the strongest general next educational step?

options.text: Assume iron deficiency and give a fixed dose.
Evaluate cause and iron status in context and plan patient blood management with appropriate timing/team review.
Transfuse every patient to a normal laboratory value.
Ignore anemia if the patient is ambulatory.

practiceQuestions.rationale: ICCAMS consensus supports identifying and assessing perioperative anemia and addressing etiology; this is not a one-size-fits-all treatment rule. [R16]

practiceQuestions.stem: What is the official board status of perioperative medicine for this fellowship?

options.text: A separate ABA perioperative medicine board exam exists.
The BWH programme guarantees eligibility for every ABA subspecialty exam.
ABA announced perioperative medicine as a content-outline topic with related questions beginning 2028; this is not a separate board certification.
No ABA exams cover perioperative concepts.

practiceQuestions.rationale: ABA overview lists general initial and subspecialty exams; 2026 announcement designates a topic within initial-certification content outline, with new questions beginning in 2028; it does not announce a standalone perioperative board. [R2][R5]

title: Neuroanesthesia Fellowship

prerequisites.level: Postgraduate physician / anesthesiology fellow-level self-study; intended for clinicians who have completed or are undertaking anesthesiology residency, not lay learners.
knowledge: general anesthetic monitoring and perioperative medicine
basic neuroanatomy, neurologic examination, ventilation and hemodynamics
introductory interpretation of EEG, evoked-potential and invasive-monitoring concepts
prerequisites.access: Read the basic SNACC four-week classroom before advanced units; no patient-care or procedural prerequisites are satisfied by this online curriculum.

objectives: Integrate cerebral physiology with perioperative anesthetic concepts while stating uncertainty and evidence limits.
Compare neuroanesthesia contexts across cranial, vascular, spine, pituitary, functional, pediatric and neurointerventional practice.
Identify high-risk changes and communicate a structured differential and escalation plan.
Appraise guidelines, consensus statements and case reports without treating educational content as patient-specific direction.
Use broad ABA anesthesiology exam-domain correlation as study organization, not as a separate board blueprint or readiness claim.

units.title: Cerebral physiology, neuroanatomy, and monitoring foundations
objectives: Explain CBF, CMRO2, autoregulation, CO2 reactivity, CPP, compliance, CSF circulation, and Monro-Kellie relationships.
Interpret common cerebral oxygenation, EEG, evoked-potential, and ICP-monitor limits without treating a number in isolation.
Connect anesthetic effects to underlying physiology and distinguish intact from injured autoregulation.
topics: arterial and venous supply; CSF; BBB
ICP/CPP measurement assumptions, cerebral oxygen delivery
basic EEG, processed EEG, TCD, NIRS, jugular bulb and brain tissue oxygenation
boardDomains: ABA ADVANCED: basic science; organ-based CNS; physics/monitoring; clinical subspecialties (broad correlation only)
units.casePractice: Interpret a fictional trend set with MAP, ICP and EEG before changing a variable; identify measurement and context limits.
units.assessment: One-page causal diagram and 5-minute oral explanation; rubric tests correct relationships, clinical qualification, and communication.

units.title: Preoperative assessment, airway, anesthetic techniques, and positioning
objectives: Organize a risk-focused preoperative review for craniotomy or neurointerventional anesthesia.
Compare general anesthesia and monitored anesthesia care by clinical goals, workflow, and patient/procedure constraints.
Recognize positioning-related venous obstruction, pressure injury, and airway/line access risks.
topics: neurologic baseline, imaging/report review, medications, seizures, antithrombotics
airway and aspiration risk; induction/emergence plan; arterial access and monitoring
prone, park-bench, lateral, sitting and head-fixed considerations; venous drainage
boardDomains: ABA ADVANCED: clinical sciences, CNS and organ-based domains, radiologic procedures, patient safety
units.casePractice: Construct a non-prescriptive preoperative checklist for a fictional elective posterior fossa case; identify items requiring surgeon or local-protocol confirmation.
units.assessment: Structured oral case: prioritization, alternatives, and stated uncertainty.

units.title: Intracranial hypertension, traumatic brain injury, and EVDs
objectives: Analyze secondary brain injury threats, including hypoxemia, hypotension, extremes of CO2, fever, and impaired venous drainage.
Summarize BTF recommendation strength and limits for ICP/CPP thresholds, ventilation and osmotherapy.
Explain safe conceptual handling of external ventricular drains and why local protocol and trained staff matter.
topics: ICP thresholds and CPP target uncertainty
EVD/lumbar drains and monitoring; waveform and artifact awareness
boardDomains: ABA ADVANCED: CNS, critical care, pharmacology, monitoring, trauma
units.casePractice: Use a fictional severe TBI timeline to identify harmful trends, evidence strength, and escalation questions for the responsible team; no treatment orders.
units.assessment: Evidence appraisal memo plus prioritization exercise; must distinguish BTF recommendation from older carried-forward statement.

units.title: Craniotomy for tumor, mass lesions, and perioperative emergencies
objectives: Plan the shared anesthetic endpoints for brain relaxation, perfusion, and timely neurologic assessment.
Recognize plausible causes of acute brain swelling, unexpected blood loss, delayed emergence, seizure, and new deficit.
Apply a structured cognitive-aid sequence to sudden intraoperative deterioration.
topics: pre-op neurologic status and steroid/antiepileptic review
brain relaxation and venous outflow; ventilation and fluid choices
emergence and immediate postoperative neurologic assessment
air embolism, venous congestion, hemorrhage, seizure, tension pneumocephalus
boardDomains: ABA ADVANCED: CNS, pharmacology, special techniques, patient safety and quality

assignment.title: Neuroanesthesia integrated reasoning portfolio (four assignments)
deliverables: A. Mechanism map: show how ventilation, arterial pressure, ICP, venous drainage, and anesthetic choice can interact; cite two primary/consensus sources.

B. Three written fictional case analyses: (i) TBI/ICP, (ii) acute stroke thrombectomy, (iii) complex-spine neuromonitoring alarm. For each separate observations, differential, escalation/communication and evidence limits.
C. Published-case critique: use the linked aneurysm case, distinguish authors’ observations from interpretation, identify uncertainty and discuss rights/privacy limits; do not reproduce figures.
D. Capstone oral-board-style simulation: 10-minute structured briefing followed by questions; no real patient data or procedural practice.

rubric.fullCredit: Correct mechanisms; cites current authoritative primary/consensus source and labels evidence strength/currentness.
rubric.partialCredit: Mostly correct but omits a qualifier or conflates evidence types.
rubric.noCredit: Major unsupported claim or treats educational scenario as clinical order.

rubric.fullCredit: Separates observed data, hypotheses, alternatives, and missing information.
rubric.partialCredit: Provides a plausible answer but with limited alternatives.
rubric.noCredit: Declares an unverified diagnosis from a single signal.

rubric.fullCredit: Names urgency, responsible team, closed-loop communication, and local protocol needs.
rubric.noCredit: Suggests unsupervised action or omits safety-critical escalation.

rubric.fullCredit: Uses links lawfully, no patient identifiers/images copied, and states course limits.
rubric.noCredit: Copies a protected image/record or implies certification.

rubric.fullCredit: Concise structured answer with clear sequence.

assignment.safety: Assignments assess knowledge expression only. They do not validate clinical judgment, procedure skills, case volume, independent practice, credentialing, or board readiness.

assessment.format: 12-unit learning portfolio with 10 original single-best-answer questions, four portfolio deliverables, and a structured fictional oral simulation.
assessment.scoringPlan: Learner self-check: score each original question with written rationale; aim for 80% for personal remediation only. Portfolio rubric totals 100 points; a suggested 80% completion threshold is an educational course-design criterion only, not a validated predictor or certification rule.
assessment.remediation: Revisit the mapped source and unit; rewrite missed rationale with evidence-strength label; discuss clinical questions with qualified faculty in an accredited training setting.
assessment.limits: Not official ABA content or leaked examination material; not a valid prediction of passing any board or proof of practice readiness.

studyHours.plan: A transparent 12-week independent study plan of 10 hours/week (120 hours total) for reading, case reflection, note synthesis, original question review, and portfolio work. This is a proposed study schedule, not clinical training time.
studyHours.note: Verified free-video watching currently contributes zero hours because candidate pages did not expose reliable total runtimes. The 36-hour video floor remains unmet; planned films are not available videos.

boardStatus.specialtyBoardExam: No separate neuroanesthesia board examination is listed by the ABA as of 2026-10-07. The MGB fellowship is reported as ICPNT-accredited; ICPNT program accreditation is not individual board certification.
boardStatus.relatedCertification: ABA separately lists Neurocritical Care subspecialty examination; it is distinct and not interchangeable with neuroanesthesia.
boardStatus.residencyBoardContext: ABA ADVANCED is a general anesthesiology examination after residency and BASIC; the public blueprint is used only for broad educational alignment, not as a neuroanesthesia fellowship blueprint.

medical.boardEligibilityNotice: This independent course does not establish ABA eligibility or board eligibility. Eligibility and certification depend on the board’s current rules and accredited training. officialProgrammes.name: Joint Mass General Brigham Neuroanesthesia Fellowship
officialProgrammes.publicCurriculumNotes: The official page says the joint physician fellowship has operated since 1992, is 12 or 18 months depending on fellow goals, is affiliated with Harvard Medical School, and was accredited by ICPNT in 2023. Listed experiences: neurosurgery operating rooms, neurointerventional radiology, neuromonitoring, neuro-ICU, neuroscience research, electives, formal didactics and conferences. The listed joint programme is treated as one track with two named hospital sites, not two duplicate specialty courses.

medical.programmeSourceScope: Official institution description is not a complete public syllabus or publicly quantified lecture schedule. ICPNT is the fellowship accreditor stated by MGB; ACGME residency requirements mention neuroanesthesia rotations but do not by themselves accredit this fellowship. No separate neuroanesthesia board exam is listed by ABA. Exact site-level rotation distribution, case volumes and fellow-specific schedule are not published in the fetched page.
sourceCaveats: The official MGB page reports 12 or 18 months but describes curriculum details for a one-year fellowship; do not assume every fellow follows the same 12-month pattern.
The official MGB page reports ICPNT accreditation in 2023; the ICPNT directory lists MGB accredited since 2023-09-07. This is not ACGME fellowship accreditation or an individual board credential.
ACGME 2026 requirements include at least two one-month neuroanesthesia rotations during anesthesiology residency; this residency requirement is distinct from the MGB neuroanesthesia fellowship.
The ABA current subspecialty list has no neuroanesthesia exam. ABA Neurocritical Care is a separate exam and must not be conflated.
The ABA ADVANCED blueprint is used only as a broad cognitive framework; no official fellowship-specific blueprint or board exam was identified.
The BTF page labels the fourth edition current, but it dates to 2016; older carried-forward statements and newer evidence require careful strength/currency reading.

SNACC curriculum and OpenAnesthesia are educational sources. OpenAnesthesia ICP page was last updated 2023-08-02. Clinical guidelines change; clinicians must consult current authoritative sources and local protocols.
A 2020 endovascular consensus full text includes pandemic-specific sections; it is retained as historical reading, not as current universal practice guidance.
The open-access aneurysm article is a consented published case; no image, clinical record or patient identifier was copied. Free access does not confer reuse rights.

Human clinical review has not been performed. This independent education resource confers no Harvard, MGB, BWH, MGH, SNACC or ICPNT affiliation; no accredited training, licensure, procedure competence, board eligibility, certification, case volume, or guaranteed passing.

practiceQuestions.stem: A fictional patient with severe TBI has an ICP rise. A learner proposes prolonged prophylactic ventilation to PaCO2 22 mm Hg as the sole measure. Which response best matches the BTF evidence summary?

options.text: Use prolonged prophylactic hyperventilation because lower ICP proves improved outcomes.
BTF advises against prolonged prophylactic hyperventilation to PaCO2 ≤25 mm Hg; a brief temporizing role is distinct from a definitive intervention.
PaCO2 has no effect on cerebral vascular tone.
Hyperventilation is the only evidence-supported treatment for all raised ICP.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The BTF fourth edition specifically does not recommend prolonged prophylactic PaCO2 ≤25 mm Hg. It restates prior edition advice about hyperventilation as a temporizing measure while noting the evidence limits. A lower ICP alone does not prove better clinical outcome.
practiceQuestions.domain: ICP / ventilation; ABA ADVANCED organ-based CNS and critical care correlation

practiceQuestions.stem: In a simplified hemodynamic model, MAP is 90 mm Hg and ICP is 25 mm Hg. Which is the usual arithmetic estimate for CPP, while retaining awareness of physiologic context?

options.text: 115 mm Hg
65 mm Hg
25 mm Hg
90 mm Hg

practiceQuestions.rationale: The commonly used approximation is CPP = MAP − ICP, so 90 − 25 = 65 mm Hg. This calculation is not a complete patient-specific interpretation; reference levels, venous pressure in selected conditions, and autoregulation matter.

practiceQuestions.stem: During a fictional craniotomy, ICP rises while oxygenation is stable. What is the best immediate reasoning approach for a supervised team?

options.text: Assume intracranial hemorrhage and ignore monitor artifact.
Check signal/context and reversible contributors, communicate with the surgeon, and evaluate evolving causes while any selected bridge is reassessed.
Set PaCO2 below 20 mm Hg for the rest of the procedure.
Give one particular hyperosmolar agent in every such case regardless of labs or hemodynamics.

practiceQuestions.rationale: A structured approach verifies the measurement and considers ventilation, blood pressure, venous outflow, positioning and surgical pathology. Treatment selection requires the responsible clinicians and local protocols; BTF does not recommend one specific hyperosmolar agent on outcome evidence.

practiceQuestions.stem: An anesthetic team prepares for endovascular thrombectomy in a fictional patient with acute ischemic stroke. Which statement about anesthetic technique is best?

options.text: General anesthesia is mandatory for every thrombectomy.
Conscious sedation is always superior.
Technique selection is individualized; the team should balance airway, neurologic cooperation, hemodynamics, workflow and reperfusion delay.
Anesthetic choice is unrelated to hemodynamics or workflow.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Clinical choice depends on patient and procedural factors. Public consensus material emphasizes communication and avoiding delays, but older pandemic-specific recommendations should not be treated as current universal targets.

practiceQuestions.stem: During a fictional spine procedure with motor-evoked-potential monitoring, a signal changes after anesthetic and physiologic changes. What should the learner do first in a systems-based discussion?

options.text: Declare an irreversible spinal cord injury from the single signal.
Use a structured team response: verify signal and technical setup, review recent anesthetic/physiologic changes, communicate with the surgeon and monitoring team, and follow local protocol.
Increase neuromuscular blockade without telling the monitoring team.
Ignore the change because evoked potentials are never useful.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Signals have technical and physiologic causes and are not themselves a definitive diagnosis. A structured, communicated response and local practice protocol are required; the learning vignette cannot authorize intervention.

practiceQuestions.stem: A fictional patient after pituitary surgery has increased urine output and a sodium change. Which inference is most defensible?

options.text: The pattern alone proves central diabetes insipidus.
The pattern requires evaluation of trends, fluid balance, relevant labs, timing and differential diagnoses with the responsible team.
No postoperative pituitary patient needs monitoring.
Treat based only on urine output without confirmation.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Postoperative fluid and sodium changes require contextual interpretation and differential diagnosis; no single observation is pathognomonic. Specific diagnosis and treatment are beyond this educational case and require clinical assessment.

practiceQuestions.stem: A student uses the 2023 BD/DNC guideline to explain a determination in a real patient. Which safeguard is essential?

options.text: Any learner can determine BD/DNC from an absent gag reflex alone.
The formal evaluation has prerequisites and defined exam/apnea/ancillary-test processes performed by appropriately qualified clinicians under current policy.
A CT image alone establishes BD/DNC.
Anesthetic and metabolic confounders do not matter.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The 2023 consensus guideline covers prerequisites, clinician qualifications, neurologic examination, apnea testing, ancillary testing, and special considerations. A self-study learner cannot determine death in a real patient.
practiceQuestions.domain: Neurocritical care, organ donation and ethics

practiceQuestions.stem: What does the ABA ADVANCED exam blueprint permit an educator to claim about this course?

options.text: It is a separate board blueprint for neuroanesthesia fellowship certification.
It is a general anesthesiology exam blueprint whose broad categories can guide educational correlation, not evidence of board eligibility or readiness.
It certifies the MGB fellowship.
It guarantees passing after completion.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The published ABA ADVANCED blueprint specifies general categories and exam format for anesthesiology. It is not a neuroanesthesia fellowship exam, and course completion cannot confer eligibility or predict passing.

practiceQuestions.stem: A trainee states that the MGB neuroanesthesia fellowship is ACGME-accredited because ACGME residency requirements mention neuroanesthesia. Which correction is accurate?

options.text: ACGME accreditation of residency and ICPNT accreditation of the MGB fellowship are distinct; the fellowship page reports ICPNT accreditation since 2023.
ACGME directly awards the ABA neuroanesthesia board.
The fellowship is not a clinical physician program.
ICPNT accreditation proves board eligibility.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The official program page and ICPNT directory report program-level ICPNT accreditation since 2023. ACGME requirements include neuroanesthesia training within anesthesiology residency; that is a distinct status and does not accredit this fellowship.

practiceQuestions.stem: A learner reads a published case report containing angiographic figures and wants to paste a figure into a course slide. What is the correct rights-aware approach?

options.text: PMC access means every image is public domain.
Link to the case and check the publisher’s license before any reuse; do not copy/rehost the image absent explicit permission or a license allowing it.
Remove the patient name and reuse the figure without attribution.
Recreate the original image and call it an educational illustration.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Free-to-view is not permission to reuse. Link to the authentic published case and verify the article/figure rights; this curriculum copies no patient images or records.
